checked.found: Dolni Vestonice fired-clay figurines dated c. 29,000-25,000 years ago (midpoint about 27,000 years ago, so -27000 is a rounded approximation); widely called the oldest fired ceramic.
Earliest quicklime/lime plaster production put at about 10,400-10,000 BCE in the Near East.
Earliest copper smelting at Belovode/Plocnik in the Balkans around 5000 BCE.
Varna Necropolis on the Black Sea coast, c. 4600-4200 BCE, with thousands of gold items.
Fired bricks appear in the fourth millennium BCE (c. 3500 BCE) in Mesopotamia and the Indus valley.
Tin bronze appears in Mesopotamia/Sumer in the later fourth to early third millennium BCE; c. 3300 BCE is a standard approximation.

Sources give mid-third millennium BCE for the earliest glass beads, but say deliberate glass production only dates from the 16th century BCE in northern Syria/Mesopotamia, and a 2016 study argues glassmaking may have begun in Egypt. The 'first man-made glass' in Mesopotamia at -2500 is contested.
Processed latex (mixed with morning glory juice) from Olmec-era El Manati, c. 1600 BCE.

The Hittite iron monopoly is now largely discredited; few iron artifacts are found in Hittite areas, most Bronze Age iron is rare or meteoritic, and iron spread gradually after the Late Bronze Age collapse. 'Producing iron weapons and tools in quantity' c. 1400 BCE is not supported.
Opus caementicium widely used from the late 3rd to 2nd century BCE with volcanic ash (pozzolana); sets underwater.
Glassblowing invented on the Syro-Palestinian coast in the mid first century BCE.
Britannica: porcelain first made in the Tang dynasty (from 618); some sources date precursors earlier.
Cristallo developed by Angelo Barovier on Murano around the mid 15th century.
Bottger produced the first European hard-paste porcelain in 1708 for Augustus the Strong, after being set to make gold.
Abraham Darby first smelted iron with coke at Coalbrookdale in 1709.
Alexander Parkes showed Parkesine at the 1862 International Exhibition in London.
Fawcett and Gibson at ICI Northwich found polyethylene in 1933 in a high-pressure experiment.
GE first reproducibly synthesised diamond in December 1954 (announced 1955).
Pilkington announced the float process in 1959 (developed through the 1950s); molten glass floated on tin.
